headings.text: Why do we need real numbers?
Dedekind cuts: one way to fill a gap

html:
The big picture

Analysis needs a number line with no gaps, because every limit needs a number to land on. The lecture starts with why \mathbb{Q} is not enough: each system in \mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R} exists to solve equations the previous one can't, and x^2 = 2 has no solution among the rational numbers, because \sqrt2 is irrational. Then it pins down what makes \mathbb{R} special: it is a complete ordered field. Field means the usual arithmetic rules. Ordered means you can compare numbers, and the inequality rules follow from that (multiplying by a negative number flips the sign). Distance comes from the absolute value, whose key rule is the triangle inequality. The inequality \lvert x-a\rvert<\varepsilon describes an interval, the \varepsilon-neighbourhood U(a,\varepsilon), which every later limit definition is built on. Complete means every nonempty set with an upper bound has a supremum (least upper bound) in \mathbb{R}; this is the least-upper-bound property. Supremum and infimum replace maximum and minimum when a bounded set doesn't contain its own edge. Two consequences follow: the Archimedean property (the natural numbers pass every real number) and the existence of n-th roots. Finally, the extended real line adds \pm\infty as symbols, not numbers.

Why do we need real numbers?

Different number systems appear because we want more equations and operations to make sense.

CountingSubtractionDivisionLimits and gaps
\mathbb{N}\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Q}\mathbb{R}
1, 2, 3, \ldotssolve x + 3 = 1solve 2x = 1solve x^2 = 2

The real numbers complete the number line.

Number systems

\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R}

Convention warning: some authors include 0 in \mathbb{N}, some do not. We state the convention when it matters.

Board. \mathbb{R} is the number system used in calculus and analysis. It contains all rational numbers and also numbers like \sqrt3 and \pi. The usual operations are +, -, \cdot, \div (division by 0 is not allowed). Examples: 1 : 2 \notin \mathbb{N} but 1 : 2 \in \mathbb{Q} (the board writes : for division); 1 + 3 = 4; the equation x^2 = 2 has no solution in \mathbb{Q}.

Board: rational vs. irrational. A real number is

  • rational if it can be written as \frac{p}{q} with p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, q \neq 0;
  • irrational if it cannot be written in this way.

Examples of irrational numbers: \sqrt2, \pi, e. Important idea: \mathbb{R} is the complete number line: informally, it has no gaps and no holes. A common approximation: \frac{22}{7} \approx \pi.

Intuition — rational and irrational

In set notation: x \in \mathbb{Q} if x = \frac{p}{q} for some p, q \in \mathbb{Z} with q \neq 0, and x is irrational if x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}. A practical test: a real number is rational exactly when its decimal expansion stops or eventually repeats (\frac{2}{7} = 0.285714\,285714\ldots). The decimals of \sqrt2 and \pi never settle into a repeating block. That is also why \frac{22}{7} = 3.142857\ldots can only approximate \pi = 3.141592\ldots: a fraction repeats, \pi doesn't, and the two already differ in the third decimal.

Connection

The Math prep course drew the same chain one step further, to \mathbb{C} for x^2 = -1: 1 Mathematical Thinking and Preliminaries (The number sets).

A quick classification game

Which set does the number belong to first?

Numbersmallest usual setcomment
5\mathbb{N}counting number
-3\mathbb{Z}integer, not natural
\frac{2}{7}\mathbb{Q}ratio of integers
\sqrt{2}\mathbb{R}real, not rational
\pi\mathbb{R}real, not rational
Common mistake — "smallest set" is not "only set"

Wrong: "5 is a natural number, so it isn't rational." The sets are nested, so 5 \in \mathbb{N} also means 5 \in \mathbb{Z}, 5 \in \mathbb{Q} (5 = \frac{5}{1}) and 5 \in \mathbb{R}. The table asks for the first set the number appears in. Read "real, not rational" as the definition of irrational: \sqrt2 \in \mathbb{R} but \sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}.

The real line

Every real number has a decimal representation, possibly infinite: -0.75, 0.333\ldots, 1.4142\ldots, \pi.

Some numbers have two decimal representations: 1 = 1.000\ldots = 0.999\ldots

Board. \frac34 = 0.75, \quad \frac13 = 0.333\ldots, \quad \pi = 3.141592\ldots

Why is 0.999\ldots equal to 1, and not just close to it?
  1. Via a known decimal: \frac13 = 0.333\ldots; multiply by 3: 1 = 0.999\ldots
  2. Via shifting: let x = 0.999\ldots Then 10x = 9.999\ldots, and 10x - x = 9, so 9x = 9 and x = 1.
  3. Via distance (this lecture's language): the gap d = 1 - 0.999\ldots is at most 1 - 0.9\ldots9 (n nines) = 10^{-n}, for every n. The only number d \ge 0 that is below every 10^{-n} is d = 0.

An infinite decimal names the number its finite truncations approach. It is not a process that "never arrives".

\sqrt{2} is not rational

The equation x^2 = 2 has a real solution, but no rational solution.

We prove this by contradiction. Assume

\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}

where p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, q \neq 0, and the fraction is in lowest terms.

If this assumption forces both p and q to be even, we have a contradiction.

Proof that \sqrt{2} is irrational

Assume \sqrt2 = \frac{p}{q} in lowest terms. Then

2 = \frac{p^2}{q^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p^2 = 2q^2.

So p^2 is even, hence p is even. Write p = 2k.

(2k)^2 = 2q^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4k^2 = 2q^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q^2 = 2k^2.

So q^2 is even, hence q is even. Thus p and q are both divisible by 2, contradicting that \frac{p}{q} was in lowest terms.

\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}.

Board. The board notes give the same proof and add why "lowest terms" is the right starting point: we may assume that the fraction is in lowest terms, so p and q are not both even. That is the statement the proof ends up contradicting.

Proof steps

What each step of the proof uses, in order:

  1. Assume \sqrt2 = \frac{p}{q} — proof by contradiction: assume the negation of the claim \sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q} (1 Elements of Logic).
  2. "in lowest terms" — every fraction can be reduced: divide p and q by their greatest common divisor. So this costs nothing.
  3. 2 = \frac{p^2}{q^2} \Rightarrow p^2 = 2q^2 — square both sides, then multiply by q^2 \neq 0.
  4. "So p^2 is even" — definition of even: p^2 = 2 \cdot q^2 with q^2 \in \mathbb{Z}.
  5. "hence p is even" — the lemma "p^2 even \Rightarrow p even" (proved in the Why below).
  6. "Write p = 2k" — definition of even again, now read the other way: some k \in \mathbb{Z} exists.
  7. 4k^2 = 2q^2 \Rightarrow q^2 = 2k^2 — substitute p = 2k into step 3, then divide by 2.
  8. "q^2 even, hence q even" — definition of even, then the same lemma as in step 5.
  9. "contradicting lowest terms" — 2 divides both p and q, but step 2 said they are not both even. The assumption in step 1 is false, so \sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}.
Why does "p^2 even" give "p even"?

Prove the contrapositive, "p odd \Rightarrow p^2 odd": if p = 2m + 1 with m \in \mathbb{Z}, then p^2 = 4m^2 + 4m + 1 = 2(2m^2 + 2m) + 1, which is odd. A statement and its contrapositive are equivalent (1 Elements of Logic), so "p^2 even \Rightarrow p even" holds too. The same argument gives "q^2 even \Rightarrow q even".

Connection

1 Elements of Logic works through this proof step by step as the model proof by contradiction. Here it has a new job: it shows that \mathbb{Q} has a hole exactly where \sqrt2 should be. That hole is what the rest of the lecture is about.

What is special about \mathbb{R}?

fieldorderedcomplete
we can add, multiply, subtract, divide by nonzero numberswe can compare numbers using < and >there are no gaps on the number line

\mathbb{R} is a complete ordered field.

Board: why "complete"? Besides the field operations and the order, the real numbers also satisfy a completeness property, which is discussed later using suprema and Dedekind cuts.

Intuition — what the three words mean

A field is a set with + and \cdot that obey the rules on slide 9, so that subtraction and division by nonzero numbers always work. An ordered field is a field with an order < that obeys the rules on slide 11. Complete is the least-upper-bound property of slide 23. \mathbb{Q} and \mathbb{R} are both ordered fields: arithmetic and comparison alone can't tell them apart. Only completeness separates them. \mathbb{Z} is not a field: 2 has no reciprocal in \mathbb{Z}.

Field properties: arithmetic rules

AdditionMultiplication
a + b = b + aab = ba
a + (b + c) = (a + b) + ca(bc) = (ab)c
a + 0 = a, \quad a + (-a) = 0a \cdot 1 = a, \quad a \cdot \frac{1}{a} = 1 \ (a \neq 0)

Connection between them: (a + b)c = ac + bc.

Intuition — names of the rules

Each rule holds for all a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}. Row by row: commutative (order doesn't matter), associative (brackets don't matter), neutral elements 0 and 1 with inverses -a and \frac1a. The connecting rule is the distributive law. Every algebraic manipulation you have ever done, such as expanding brackets or cancelling, is a chain of these few rules.

Subtraction and division

Subtraction is addition of the opposite: a - b := a + (-b). Example: 7 - 10 = 7 + (-10) = -3.

Division is multiplication by the reciprocal: \frac{a}{b} := a \cdot \frac{1}{b}, b \neq 0. Example: \frac{6}{3} = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 2.

Division by 0 is not defined.

Why can't we divide by 0?

\frac{a}{0} would mean a \cdot \frac{1}{0}, so we would need a number \frac10 with 0 \cdot \frac10 = 1. But 0 \cdot x = 0 for every x. This follows from the field rules: 0 \cdot x = (0 + 0)x = 0x + 0x, and adding -(0x) to both sides gives 0 = 0x. So no number can serve as \frac10. Allowing it anyway would force 1 = 0.

Ordering

For any two real numbers a, b, exactly one of the following is true: a < b, a = b, a > b.

  • If a < b, then a + c < b + c. Adding the same number preserves order.
  • If a < b and c < 0, then ac > bc. Multiplying by a negative number reverses order.
Why does multiplying by a negative number reverse the order?

Use two facts: x < y means y - x > 0, and a product of two positive numbers is positive (part of what "ordered field" means).

  1. Translate into positivity: a < b gives b - a > 0; c < 0 gives -c > 0.
  2. Multiply the two positives: (b - a)(-c) > 0, i.e. ac - bc > 0.
  3. Translate back: ac > bc.

As a picture: multiplying by -1 mirrors the line at 0, and a mirror swaps left and right.

Quick check: inequalities

Start with 2 < 5.

  • Add 3: 2 + 3 < 5 + 3, i.e. 5 < 8, true.
  • Multiply by -2: -4 \ ? \ -10. Answer: -4 > -10.

When multiplying by a negative number, flip the inequality sign.

Board. If x < y, then 3x < 3y but -3x > -3y. Multiplying by a positive number preserves the inequality; multiplying by a negative number reverses it.

Worked example — solving a linear inequality

Solve 3 - 2x < 7.

  1. Isolate the x-term (add -3; adding preserves order): -2x < 4.
  2. Divide by -2. Dividing is multiplying by -\frac12 < 0, so flip the sign: x > -2.
  3. Write as an interval (slide 15): x \in (-2, \infty).
  4. Check with test points: x = 0 gives 3 < 7 ✓; x = -3 gives 9 < 7 ✗. That matches.
Common mistake — multiplying by something whose sign you don't know

Wrong: from \frac{1}{x} < 2, multiply by x to get 1 < 2x, so x > \frac12. That step multiplied by x without knowing its sign. Counterexample: x = -1 satisfies \frac{1}{x} = -1 < 2 but not x > \frac12. Right approach: split into cases. If x > 0, keep the sign: x > \frac12. If x < 0, flip it: 1 > 2x, which every negative x satisfies. Solution: x \in (-\infty, 0) \cup (\frac12, \infty).

Absolute value as distance

For a \in \mathbb{R}, the absolute value is

\lvert a \rvert = \begin{cases} a, & a \ge 0, \\ -a, & a < 0. \end{cases}
  • \lvert x \rvert = distance from x to 0.
  • \lvert x - a \rvert = distance from x to a.

Board. Example: \lvert 3 - (-2) \rvert = \lvert 5 \rvert = 5, the distance between 3 and -2 on the line.

Intuition — the minus sign in "-a"

For a < 0, the number -a is positive: \lvert -3 \rvert = -(-3) = 3. Read "-a" as "the opposite of a", not "a negative number". Two equivalent forms that help in proofs: \lvert a \rvert = \max(a, -a) and \lvert a \rvert = \sqrt{a^2}.

Absolute value: useful properties

For a, b \in \mathbb{R}:

  • \lvert a \rvert \ge 0, and \lvert a \rvert = 0 \iff a = 0.
  • \lvert -a \rvert = \lvert a \rvert, and \lvert ab \rvert = \lvert a \rvert\, \lvert b \rvert.

Triangle inequality:

\lvert a + b \rvert \le \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert.

The distance of a two-part trip is at most the sum of the two distances.

Board. Geometric meaning: one side of a triangle is not longer than the sum of the other two sides. For a triangle with sides a, b, c: c \le a + b.

Why does the triangle inequality hold?
  1. Sandwich each number: -\lvert a \rvert \le a \le \lvert a \rvert and -\lvert b \rvert \le b \le \lvert b \rvert (one side is an equality, the other compares a negative with a positive number).
  2. Add the two sandwiches (adding the same number twice preserves order): -(\lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert) \le a + b \le \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert.
  3. Read it as a distance: a + b lies within distance \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert of 0. Since \lvert y \rvert \le c \iff -c \le y \le c, this says exactly \lvert a + b \rvert \le \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert.

Equality holds exactly when a and b don't have opposite signs.

Common mistake — \lvert a + b \rvert = \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert

Tempting, because the product rule \lvert ab \rvert = \lvert a \rvert\,\lvert b \rvert does hold. For sums it fails as soon as the signs differ: a = 2, b = -3 gives \lvert a + b \rvert = 1 but \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert = 5. Steps in opposite directions partly cancel, which is why the rule is only "\le".

Intervals

An interval is a subset of the real line that contains all real numbers between any two of its elements.

NotationConditionPicture
(a, b)a < x < bopen endpoints
[a, b]a \le x \le bclosed endpoints
[a, b)a \le x < bclosed left, open right
(a, \infty)x > aray
(-\infty, b]x \le bray

Board: intervals as sets.

\begin{aligned} (a, b) &:= \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x < b\}, \\ [a, b] &:= \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}, \\ [a, b) &:= \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x < b\}, \\ (a, b] &:= \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x \le b\}. \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • a, b \in \mathbb{R} — the endpoints, a < b (for [a, b] also a = b is allowed: [a, a] = \{a\})
  • ( or ) — the endpoint is not in the interval (open end); [ or ] — the endpoint is in it (closed end)
  • := — "is defined as"; \{x \in \mathbb{R} : \ldots\} — the set of all real x with the property after the colon (2 Elements of Sets)
  • \pm\infty as an endpoint (next line) — always with a round bracket: \pm\infty is not a real number, so the interval can't contain it (Extended real line)

Further examples: (a, \infty), [a, \infty), (-\infty, \infty) = \mathbb{R}, (-\infty, b], (-\infty, b).

Board: example. Solve \lvert x + 1 \rvert < 2. This is equivalent to -2 < x + 1 < 2, and therefore -3 < x < 1. So the solution set is x \in (-3, 1).

Solving an inequality often means finding an interval.

Quick check: inequality to interval

Solve \lvert x - 3 \rvert < 0.5.

This means: the distance from x to 3 is less than 0.5, so 3 - 0.5 < x < 3 + 0.5.

So 2.5 < x < 3.5, i.e. x \in (2.5, 3.5).

\lvert x - a \rvert < \varepsilon describes an interval around a.

Worked example — absolute-value inequalities, "<" and "≥"

(a) \lvert 2x - 1 \rvert < 3.

  1. Unpack the absolute value (\lvert y \rvert < c \iff -c < y < c): -3 < 2x - 1 < 3.
  2. Isolate x in all three parts (add 1, then divide by 2 > 0, no flip): -1 < x < 2.
  3. Write the interval: x \in (-1, 2).
  4. Check with the distance picture: \lvert 2x - 1 \rvert = 2\,\lvert x - \tfrac12 \rvert < 3 means x is within 1.5 of \tfrac12, i.e. between -1 and 2 ✓.

(b) \lvert x + 2 \rvert \ge 1.

  1. Read it as a distance: \lvert x - (-2) \rvert \ge 1, so x is at least 1 away from -2.
  2. Split into two pieces (\lvert y \rvert \ge c \iff y \le -c or y \ge c): x + 2 \le -1 or x + 2 \ge 1, i.e. x \le -3 or x \ge -1.
  3. Write the answer: x \in (-\infty, -3] \cup [-1, \infty). That is two rays, not one interval.
Common mistake — writing a "≥" inequality as one chain

Wrong: \lvert x + 2 \rvert \ge 1 \ \Rightarrow\ -1 \ge x + 2 \ge 1. That chain would need -1 \ge 1, so it describes the empty set. "Less than" gives and: one interval around the centre. "Greater than" gives or: two rays pointing outward.

Neighbourhoods

For a \in \mathbb{R} and \varepsilon > 0, the \varepsilon-neighbourhood of a is

U(a, \varepsilon) := (a - \varepsilon,\ a + \varepsilon).

x \in U(a, \varepsilon) \iff \lvert x - a \rvert < \varepsilon.

Board. U(a, \varepsilon) is also denoted by B_\varepsilon(a). The closed \varepsilon-neighbourhood is

\overline{U}(a, \varepsilon) = \overline{B}_\varepsilon(a) = [a - \varepsilon,\ a + \varepsilon].
Symbols
  • a \in \mathbb{R} — the centre; \varepsilon > 0 — the radius
  • B_\varepsilon(a) — another name for U(a, \varepsilon) ("B" for ball, the name used in higher dimensions, where the neighbourhood is a disc or a ball)
  • the bar in \overline{U}, \overline{B} — "closed": the two endpoints a \pm \varepsilon now belong to the set

Examples: U(2, 0.1) = (1.9,\ 2.1), \quad U(0, 5) = (-5,\ 5).

Intuition

Think "target value a with tolerance \pm\varepsilon". A machined part with nominal length a passes inspection if its length lies in U(a, \varepsilon), and a smaller \varepsilon is a stricter tolerance. The endpoints are left out (open circles), so every point of U(a, \varepsilon) still has a little room around it inside U.

Connection

This is the shape of every limit definition ahead: "a_n converges to a" will mean that for every \varepsilon > 0, all terms from some index on lie in U(a, \varepsilon). That is a \forall \varepsilon\ \exists N\ \forall n statement, exactly the kind of nested quantifiers practised in 1 Elements of Logic.

Bounded sets in \mathbb{R}

Let S \subseteq \mathbb{R}.

Bounded from above: \exists M \in \mathbb{R}\ \ \forall s \in S:\ s \le M. Then M is an upper bound.

Bounded from below: \exists m \in \mathbb{R}\ \ \forall s \in S:\ m \le s. Then m is a lower bound.

A set is bounded if it is bounded from above and below.

Bounds do not have to belong to the set.

Board. S is unbounded if it is not bounded. Examples:

  • (0, 1) is bounded. Lower bounds include 0, -1, -10, \ldots and upper bounds include 1, 2, \ldots
  • [1, 2] is bounded.
  • (0, \infty) and \mathbb{N} are bounded from below, but not from above.
  • \mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Q} and \mathbb{R} are unbounded (neither from below nor from above).
  • \{x \in \mathbb{R} : -1 \le \sin x \le 1\} = \mathbb{R}, so it is unbounded.
  • \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 \le 1\} = [-1, 1], hence bounded.
  • \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 \ge 1\} = (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty), hence unbounded.
Intuition — read the condition, not the set-builder

The last three examples look alike but behave differently. Work out which x pass the test before judging boundedness. -1 \le \sin x \le 1 holds for every real x, so the set is all of \mathbb{R}, even though the numbers \pm1 appear in the condition. x^2 \le 1 means \lvert x \rvert \le 1 (one interval, distance at most 1 from 0), while x^2 \ge 1 means \lvert x \rvert \ge 1 (two rays, the same and/or split as in the absolute-value example above). Note too that "unbounded" only needs one side to fail: \mathbb{N} is unbounded although it is bounded from below.

Intuition

An upper bound is a ceiling for S: no element sticks out above it. Any number above a ceiling is also a ceiling, so a set bounded from above always has infinitely many upper bounds. The interesting question is which one is the lowest. Example: for S = (0, 1), the numbers 1, 2 and 100 are upper bounds; 0.9 is not, because 0.95 \in S.

Common mistake — negating "bounded from above"

"Not bounded from above" is not "\exists M\ \forall s \in S: s > M" (that would say every element is above one fixed number). Negate quantifier by quantifier, as in chapter 1: \forall M \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists s \in S:\ s > M. Every candidate ceiling is beaten by some element. Example: \mathbb{N} is not bounded from above; that is the Archimedean property (slide 25).

Minimum and maximum

A number a \in S is the minimum of S if a \le s for all s \in S. A number b \in S is the maximum of S if s \le b for all s \in S.

  • S = [0, 1]: \min S = 0, \max S = 1.
  • S = (0, 1): no minimum, no maximum.

A minimum or maximum must be an element of the set.

Supremum and infimum

The supremum of S is the least upper bound. The infimum of S is the greatest lower bound.

For S = (0, 1) we have \inf S = 0, \sup S = 1. But S has no minimum and no maximum.

Board. For the empty set, one often writes in the extended real line: \inf \emptyset = +\infty, \sup \emptyset = -\infty. For unbounded sets one may also use \inf S = -\infty or \sup S = +\infty.

Why would \sup \emptyset be -\infty, the smallest possible value?

Every real number M is an upper bound of \emptyset: "s \le M for all s \in \emptyset" has no s to check, so it is true (vacuous truth, 1 Elements of Logic). The upper bounds are therefore all of \mathbb{R}, and there is no least one in \mathbb{R}. In \overline{\mathbb{R}} the least element of "everything" is -\infty, so \sup \emptyset = -\infty. By the mirror argument every real number is a lower bound, and the greatest is +\infty. That is why the convention looks upside down: for every nonempty set \inf S \le \sup S, and only \emptyset breaks this.

Intuition

Collect all upper bounds of S; the supremum is the lowest of them, the tightest ceiling. It sits exactly at the top edge of S, whether or not that edge belongs to S. If the edge does belong to S, it is the maximum and \sup S = \max S. So the supremum is the version of "maximum" that still works when the edge is open. The infimum is the same idea at the bottom edge.

Why does "\max S exists" give \sup S = \max S?

b = \max S is an upper bound by definition. Any smaller number c < b fails to be an upper bound, because b \in S and b > c. So b is the least upper bound.

Formal view of supremum

A number \beta \in \mathbb{R} is the supremum of S if:

  • s \le \beta for all s \in S,
  • and every smaller number fails to be an upper bound.

Equivalent \varepsilon-form:

\forall \varepsilon > 0 \quad \exists s \in S: \quad s > \beta - \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • S — the set whose supremum we want, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}
  • \beta — the candidate supremum (already known to be an upper bound of S)
  • \varepsilon — any positive number, however small: how far below \beta we look
  • s — an element of S that lies above \beta - \varepsilon, i.e. within \varepsilon of \beta

You can get arbitrarily close to the supremum from inside the set.

Why is the \varepsilon-form the same as "every smaller number fails to be an upper bound"?

Every number smaller than \beta can be written as \beta - \varepsilon with \varepsilon > 0. "\beta - \varepsilon is not an upper bound" is the negation of \forall s \in S: s \le \beta - \varepsilon, which is \exists s \in S: s > \beta - \varepsilon. Saying this for every smaller number means saying it for every \varepsilon > 0. So the two conditions are the same statement, once in the language of bounds and once in the language of distance.

Formal view of infimum

Board. A number \alpha \in \mathbb{R} is the infimum of S if

  1. \alpha \le s for all s \in S (so \alpha is a lower bound), and
  2. every larger number fails to be a lower bound.

Equivalently,

\forall \varepsilon > 0 \quad \exists s \in S: \quad s < \alpha + \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • S \subseteq \mathbb{R} — the set whose infimum we want
  • \alpha — the candidate infimum (already known to be a lower bound of S)
  • \varepsilon — any positive number, however small: how far above \alpha we look
  • s — an element of S that lies below \alpha + \varepsilon, i.e. within \varepsilon of \alpha
Intuition — the supremum test, mirrored

Swap every "above" for "below": \le turns into \ge, "smaller" into "larger", \beta - \varepsilon into \alpha + \varepsilon. Example: S = (0, 1), \alpha = 0. Given \varepsilon > 0, the element s = \min(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, \frac12) lies in S and below 0 + \varepsilon. So nothing above 0 is a lower bound, and \inf S = 0.

Quick check: bounds

Complete the table.

Set S\inf S\sup S\min S\max S
[0, 1]0101

(0, \infty)0does not existdoes not existdoes not exist

Worked example — find and justify inf, sup, min, max

S = \{1 - \frac{1}{n} : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n \ge 1\} = \{0, \frac12, \frac23, \frac34, \ldots\}.

  1. List elements and guess: the elements start at 0 and increase towards 1. Guess \min S = \inf S = 0, \sup S = 1, no maximum.
  2. Minimum: 0 \in S (take n = 1) and 1 - \frac1n \ge 0 for all n \ge 1. So 0 is the minimum, and therefore also the infimum.
  3. Upper bound: 1 - \frac1n < 1 for all n, so 1 is an upper bound. It is never reached (that would need \frac1n = 0), so there is no maximum.
  4. Least upper bound (\varepsilon-form): given \varepsilon > 0, choose n > \frac{1}{\varepsilon} (possible by the Archimedean property, slide 25). Then \frac1n < \varepsilon, so s = 1 - \frac1n > 1 - \varepsilon. Example: \varepsilon = 0.01, n = 101 gives s = \frac{100}{101} \approx 0.9901 > 0.99.
  5. Conclude: \sup S = 1; \max S does not exist.
Common mistake — "the supremum must be in the set"

Wrong: "\sup (0, 1) doesn't exist because 1 \notin (0, 1)." That mixes up supremum and maximum. The supremum is a bound, and bounds don't have to belong to the set (slide 18). Ask two separate questions: where is the top edge? (that's the supremum) and does the set contain it? (only then is it also the maximum).

Completeness: no gaps

Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded from above has a least upper bound in \mathbb{R}.

This is the least-upper-bound property.

  • In \mathbb{Q}, the set \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2,\ q > 0\} has no rational supremum.
  • In \mathbb{R}, the same gap is filled by \sqrt{2}.

Board. In \mathbb{Q}, the set A = \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2,\ q > 0\} does not have a rational supremum. In \mathbb{R}, the analogous set A = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 2,\ x > 0\} has \sup A = \sqrt2 \in \mathbb{R}. This illustrates the completeness of the real numbers.

Completeness is what distinguishes \mathbb{R} from \mathbb{Q}.

Intuition

\mathbb{Q} is like a ruler with infinitely many, arbitrarily fine tick marks that still has pin-holes at \sqrt2, \pi, and so on. Completeness says \mathbb{R} has no pin-holes: whenever a set bounded from above piles up against an edge, a real number sits at that edge. This is what makes limits work: 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \ldots approaches a number in \mathbb{R}, but none in \mathbb{Q}. The mirror statement also holds: every nonempty set that is bounded from below has an infimum in \mathbb{R}.

Why does \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2,\ q > 0\} have no rational supremum?

Call the set A, and suppose some rational r > 0 were its least upper bound. r^2 = 2 is impossible (\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}), which leaves two cases:

  1. r^2 < 2: a slightly larger rational still has square < 2. It lies in A and above r, so r was not an upper bound.
  2. r^2 > 2: a slightly smaller rational still has square > 2. It is still an upper bound and lies below r, so r was not the least one.

Both cases give a contradiction. The edge of A is at \sqrt2, and \mathbb{Q} has nothing there. With numbers: 1.4^2 = 1.96 < 2, while \frac{17}{12} \approx 1.4167 has (\frac{17}{12})^2 = \frac{289}{144} \approx 2.007 > 2. Rationals close in on the edge from both sides but never hit it.

Common mistake — forgetting the hypotheses

The property needs nonempty and bounded from above. (0, \infty) is not bounded from above and has no supremum in \mathbb{R} (slide 22: "does not exist"). \emptyset has none in \mathbb{R} either: every real number is an upper bound of \emptyset, and there is no least one. (The board's \sup (0, \infty) = +\infty and \sup \emptyset = -\infty are values in \overline{\mathbb{R}}, not real suprema, so they don't contradict this.) And the property promises a supremum, never a maximum: (0, 1) is bounded from above but has no maximum.

Dedekind cuts: one way to fill a gap

A cut separates numbers into a left part and a right part: A \mid B, where every a \in A is less than every b \in B.

For rational numbers, a cut can represent a missing number such as \sqrt{2}.

Board. A cut splits the line into two parts A \mid B such that every element of A lies to the left of every element of B. For example, for a fixed \alpha \in \mathbb{R}:

A = \{x : x \le \alpha\}, \qquad B = \{x : x > \alpha\}.
Symbols
  • \alpha \in \mathbb{R} — the fixed point where the line is cut
  • A — the left part, here including \alpha; B — the right part; x ranges over \mathbb{R}

Then A has the greatest element \alpha, and B has no smallest element.

Completeness means, informally, that there are no gaps. The following gap-like situations do not occur in \mathbb{R}:

  • A has a greatest number and B has a smallest number, separated by a gap;
  • A has no greatest element and B has no smallest element.
Why can neither situation happen for a cut of \mathbb{R}?

Take a cut A \mid B of the whole line: every real number is in A or in B, both parts nonempty.

  1. Both ends present: if a = \max A and b = \min B, then a < b, and the midpoint m = \frac{a + b}{2} satisfies a < m < b. m is not in A (it is above \max A) and not in B (it is below \min B). That contradicts "every number is in A or B".
  2. Both ends missing: every b \in B is an upper bound of A, so A is nonempty and bounded from above, and completeness gives s = \sup A \in \mathbb{R}. If s \in A, it is the greatest element of A. If s \in B, it is the smallest element of B, because every b \in B is an upper bound of A and so b \ge s. Either way one end is present.

So in \mathbb{R} exactly one of the two parts has its edge point, as in the board's example. In \mathbb{Q}, step 2 fails: the cut at \sqrt2 in the Intuition below has both ends missing.

Intuition

A Dedekind cut splits \mathbb{Q} into a left part A and a right part B, with everything in A below everything in B. If the split happens at a rational number, that number sits on the border. If it happens at a hole, for example A = \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \le 0 \text{ or } q^2 < 2\} and B = \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q > 0,\ q^2 > 2\}, then no rational sits on the border, and the cut itself is taken as the new number \sqrt2. Building \mathbb{R} this way means one real number per cut. You won't need the construction itself. Its point is that "no gaps" can be built from \mathbb{Q} rather than just assumed.

Archimedean property

For every real number a, there exists a natural number n such that n > a.

In words: natural numbers eventually pass any fixed real number.

Corollary: if 0 < a < b, then there exists n \in \mathbb{N} such that na > b.

Small repeated steps can eventually pass any fixed distance.

Why does it hold, and why does it need completeness?

Suppose not: some a has n \le a for all n \in \mathbb{N}. Then \mathbb{N} is nonempty and bounded from above, so by completeness s = \sup \mathbb{N} exists. s - 1 is smaller than s, so it is not an upper bound: some n \in \mathbb{N} has n > s - 1. Then n + 1 > s, and n + 1 \in \mathbb{N}. That contradicts s being an upper bound of \mathbb{N}.

Corollary: apply the property to the real number \frac{b}{a} to get n > \frac{b}{a}, then multiply by a > 0 (no flip): na > b.

Worked example — the step you'll use most: making \frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon

Claim: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an n \in \mathbb{N} with \frac1n < \varepsilon.

  1. Apply the Archimedean property to \frac{1}{\varepsilon}: choose n > \frac{1}{\varepsilon}.
  2. Rearrange (multiply both sides by \frac{\varepsilon}{n} > 0, no flip): \varepsilon > \frac{1}{n}.
  3. Concrete numbers: \varepsilon = 0.001 needs n > 1000, e.g. n = 1001.

This is step 4 of the supremum example above, and it reappears in every proof that \frac1n approaches 0. The corollary in numbers: steps of a = 0.001 pass b = 1000 after n = 1\,000\,001 steps (n = 10^6 reaches exactly 1000, not more).

Connection

The statement \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}: n > x was the worked negation example in 1 Elements of Logic. There its truth was taken for granted; here it gets a name and a reason.

Roots and rational powers

For a \ge 0 and n \in \mathbb{N}, an n-th root of a is a number r \ge 0 such that

r^n = a.

We write

r = \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n}.

For a > 0 and r = \frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{Q},

a^r := \sqrt[n]{a^m}.
Symbols
  • a — the number we take the root or power of (a \ge 0 for roots, a > 0 for rational powers)
  • n — the order of the root (n = 2: square root, n = 3: cube root); a natural number n \ge 1
  • r — in the first two lines, the root itself (a real number \ge 0); in the last line, a rational exponent r = \frac{m}{n}. The slide uses the same letter for both.
  • m — numerator of the exponent, an integer m \in \mathbb{Z}
  • \sqrt[n]{\ \cdot\ }, a^{1/n} — two notations for the same n-th root
Unclear (slide 26)

Two conditions are left implicit: n must be at least 1 (n = 0 would ask for r^0 = 1 = a, which only works for a = 1; it matters if \mathbb{N} includes 0, see slide 3), and in r = \frac{m}{n} the numerator is an integer, m \in \mathbb{Z}. The slide also reuses r for the root and for the exponent.

Why does the n-th root exist in \mathbb{R}, and why is there only one?

Existence: take a \ge 0, n \ge 1, and S = \{x \ge 0 : x^n \le a\}. S is nonempty (0 \in S) and bounded from above by \max(1, a): if x > 1 and x > a, then x^n \ge x > a. By completeness, r = \sup S exists, and one shows r^n = a (both r^n < a and r^n > a lead to the same kind of contradiction as for \sqrt2 on slide 23). Uniqueness: if 0 \le r_1 < r_2, then r_1^n < r_2^n, so at most one r \ge 0 can satisfy r^n = a.

In \mathbb{Q} the same set can have no supremum, and that is exactly the \sqrt2 hole again.

Board. In particular, \sqrt[2]{a} = \sqrt{a} (square root) and \sqrt[3]{a} (cube root). For a, b \ge 0,

\sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]{a} \cdot \sqrt[n]{b}.
Symbols
  • a, b \ge 0 — the two factors; n \ge 1 — the order of the root, as above

But in general, \sqrt{a + b} \neq \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}. Example: \sqrt{16 + 9} = \sqrt{25} = 5, whereas \sqrt{16} + \sqrt{9} = 4 + 3 = 7.

Board: rational exponents. If r = \frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{Q} and a > 0, then

a^r = a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^m.

Symbols as above. Examples: 16^{1/2} = 4, \quad 27^{1/3} = 3, \quad 8^{2/3} = \left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 4.

Intuition — evaluating a rational power

The last form, \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^m, is usually the easier one: take the root first and the numbers stay small. 27^{4/3} = \left(\sqrt[3]{27}\right)^4 = 3^4 = 81, while the other order needs \sqrt[3]{27^4} = \sqrt[3]{531441}. Roots split over products but not over sums, because a root is a power (\sqrt{a} = a^{1/2}), and powers satisfy (ab)^{1/2} = a^{1/2} b^{1/2} but have no rule for (a + b)^{1/2}.

Common mistake — \sqrt{4} = \pm 2 and \sqrt{x^2} = x

By definition the root is the number r \ge 0, so \sqrt4 = 2, full stop. The equation x^2 = 4 has two solutions, x = \pm\sqrt4 = \pm 2: the \pm comes from solving the equation, not from the root. For the same reason \sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x \rvert, not x. Try x = -3: \sqrt{9} = 3.

Extended real line

Sometimes we add two symbols:

\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}.
Symbols
  • \overline{\mathbb{R}} — the extended real line (read "R bar")
  • +\infty, -\infty — two symbols placed "above" and "below" every real number; they are not real numbers
  • \cup — union of sets (2 Elements of Sets)

Board: some formal rules.

\begin{aligned} +\infty + (+\infty) &= +\infty, \\ -\infty - \infty &= -\infty, \\ (+\infty) \cdot (+\infty) &= +\infty, \\ (+\infty) \cdot (-\infty) &= -\infty, \\ (-\infty) \cdot (-\infty) &= +\infty. \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. The board's undefined examples: +\infty - (+\infty) and \frac{+\infty}{\infty}. These symbols are useful when talking about bounds, limits, and unbounded sets.

They are useful for limits, bounds, and improper integrals. But they are not ordinary real numbers. Some expressions are not defined:

\infty - \infty, \qquad 0 \cdot \infty, \qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

Symbols as above.

Treat \pm\infty as useful symbols, not as usual numbers.

Why are \infty - \infty, 0 \cdot \infty and \frac{\infty}{\infty} undefined?

Read \infty as "something that grows without bound". n, n + 1 and 2n all grow without bound, yet (n + 1) - n = 1, 2n - n = n (grows without bound) and n - n = 0. So "\infty - \infty" could come out as anything. Likewise \frac{n}{2n} = \frac12 but \frac{n^2}{n} = n ("\frac{\infty}{\infty}"), and \frac1n \cdot n = 1 but \frac1n \cdot n^2 = n ("0 \cdot \infty"). No single value would be right every time, so none is assigned. Expressions without this ambiguity, such as \infty + \infty = \infty or a + \infty = \infty for real a, are allowed.

Connection

This is where the board's conventions \sup S = +\infty (for a set that isn't bounded from above, e.g. \sup (0, \infty) = +\infty) and \sup \emptyset = -\infty live (Supremum and infimum). The slide-22 table works inside \mathbb{R} and says "does not exist". Both describe the same situation; the lecturer uses both, so say which one you mean, and check which one an exercise expects.

Key Facts

Number systems

  • \mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R}
  • \sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}
  • \mathbb{R} fills the gaps of \mathbb{Q}.
  • \mathbb{R} is represented by the real line.

Distance and intervals

  • \lvert x \rvert is distance from x to 0.
  • \lvert x - a \rvert is distance from x to a.
  • U(a, \varepsilon) = (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon)
  • x \in U(a, \varepsilon) \iff \lvert x - a \rvert < \varepsilon.

Structure of \mathbb{R}

  • \mathbb{R} is a complete ordered field.
  • Arithmetic: +, \cdot, -, / for nonzero divisors.
  • Order: a < b, a = b, or a > b.
  • Completeness: no missing points.

Bounds

  • \min S, \max S \in S if they exist.
  • \inf S, \sup S need not belong to S.
  • Every nonempty S \subseteq \mathbb{R} bounded above has \sup S \in \mathbb{R}.
  • Every fixed a \in \mathbb{R} is smaller than some n \in \mathbb{N}.
